title: Simplified and Faster Algorithms for the Directed Single/Dual-Failure Replacement Paths via Modulo-Layer Hitting Sets

paper.title: Simplified and Faster Algorithms for the Directed Single/Dual-Failure Replacement Paths via Modulo-Layer Hitting Sets
paper.abstract: Abstract We study the replacement paths problem in unweighted directed graphs with n n vertices and m m edges under one or two edge failures. We give simpler and faster algorithms for both settings. Both algorithms are based on a new technique, which we call modulo-layer hitting sets . For the single-failure setting, we obtain a simple deterministic combinatorial algorithm running in O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(m\sqrt{n}) time, which is nearly optimal under the combinatorial Boolean Matrix Multiplication (BMM) conjecture. In addition to removing the logarithmic overhead of the deterministic O ~ ​ ( m ​ n ) \tilde{O}(m\sqrt{n}) -time † † † The O ~ ​ ( ⋅ ) \tilde{O}(\cdot) notation hides polylogarithmic factors, i.e., O ~ ​ ( f ⁡ ( n ) ) = O ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( n ) ​ polylog ​ ( n ) ) \tilde{O}(f(n))=O(f(n)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)) . algorithm of Alon, Chechik, and Cohen [ICALP’19], our algorithm admits a much simpler implementation and analysis. For the dual-failure setting, we obtain a randomized combinatorial algorithm running in O ~ ​ ( n 3 − 1 / 4 ) \tilde{O}(n^{3-1/4}) time. This improves upon the previous O ~ ​ ( n 3 − 1 / 18 ) \tilde{O}(n^{3-1/18}) -time combinatorial algorithm of Chechik and Zhang [ICALP’24].

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In the replacement paths problem, we study how shortest paths change under edge failure. Specifically, given an unweighted directed graph G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) with n n vertices and m m edges and two vertices s , t ∈ V s,t\in V , the classical replacement paths (RP) problem asks to compute, for every edge e ∈ E e\in E , a shortest s s - t t path that avoids e e . Its natural two-failure extension, the dual-failure replacement paths (2-FRP) problem, asks to compute, for every pair of edges e , e ′ ∈ E e,e^{\prime}\in E , a shortest s s - t t path that avoids both e e and e ′ e^{\prime} . The replacement paths problem has been extensively studied in the literature [ MMG89 , NPW01 , HSB07 , GL09 , EPR10 , WN10 , Ber10 , EN11 , Wil11 , RZ12 , WY13 , LL14 , GW19 , CN20 , VWX22 , CZ24a , MR24 , CCD+25 , NV26 , HI26 ] , motivated in part by its role as a basic model for fault-tolerant routing. In real-world networks, links may become unavailable due to failures, and it is desirable to quickly find alternative routes while preserving shortest-path guarantees. Replacement paths naturally capture this task by computing shortest routes that remain available after such failures. Beyond this networking motivation, replacement paths are also closely connected to several fundamental problems. In particular, replacement paths arise in computing Vickrey pricing for shortest paths in algorithmic mechanism design (see [ NR99 , HS01 ] ). They are also closely related to the k k shortest paths problem, which is itself a classical and well-studied problem [ Law72 , Epp98 ] . For the classical RP problem, the complexity differs significantly between undirected and directed graphs. Note that the output size of RP is only Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(n) , since it suffices to consider failures of edges on a fixed shortest s s – t t path. For undirected graphs, RP can be solved essentially as efficiently as single-source shortest paths [ MMG89 , LL14 ] . In contrast, RP on directed graphs appears substantially harder. For unweighted directed graphs, Roditty and Zwick [ RZ12 ] gave a randomized combinatorial algorithm running in O ~ ​ ( m ​ n ) \tilde{O}(m\sqrt{n}) time. Obtaining a deterministic algorithm with a comparable running time remained open for more than a decade, until Alon, Chechik, and Cohen [ ACC19 ] gave a deterministic O ~ ​ ( m ​ n ) \tilde{O}(m\sqrt{n}) -time combinatorial algorithm. This running time is optimal up to n o ⁡ ( 1 ) n^{o(1)} factor among combinatorial algorithms, assuming the combinatorial Boolean Matrix Multiplication (BMM) conjecture [ WW18 ] . For weighted directed graphs, RP is subcubic-equivalent to APSP [ WW18 ] . ‡ ‡ ‡ Very recently, Alman and Vassilevska Williams [ AW26 ] gave a truly subcubic O ⁡ ( n 2.9995 ) O(n^{2.9995}) -time algorithm for APSP on directed graphs with polynomially bounded integer weights, refuting the APSP hypothesis. By the subcubic equivalence [ WW18 ] , RP on weighted directed graphs is thus also solvable in truly subcubic time. Their algorithm relies on fast matrix multiplication and is not combinatorial. In particular, the conditional lower bounds in this paper based on the combinatorial BMM conjecture are unaffected. For algebraic algorithms, Vassilevska Williams [ Wil11 ] gave a randomized O ~ ​ ( M ​ n ω ) \tilde{O}(Mn^{\omega}) -time algorithm § § § Here, ω \omega denotes the exponent of square matrix multiplication. The current best bound over an arbitrary fixed field is ω < 2.37106 \omega<2.37106 [ ADV+25 , DEK+26 , Ope26a ] . Over the complex numbers, the stronger bound ω ⁡ ( ℂ ) ≤ 9 / 4 \omega(\mathbb{C})\leq 9/4 was recently established [ Ope26b ] . for edge weights in { − M , … , M } \{-M,\ldots,M\} . Although the notion of a “combinatorial algorithm” is not formally defined, here and throughout we use the term informally to refer to algorithms that do not rely on fast matrix multiplication, such as Strassen-like methods. Such algorithms are often viewed as more efficient in practice, since fast matrix multiplication algorithms typically involve large hidden constants. We refer the reader to [ AFK+24 , Section 1.1] for a more extensive discussion of the motivations for seeking combinatorial algorithms, as well as for possible operational definitions of this notion. The 2-FRP problem is considerably less understood. Vassilevska Williams, Woldeghebriel, and Xu [ VWX22 ] gave a O ~ ​ ( n 3 ) \tilde{O}(n^{3}) -time algorithm for weighted directed graphs and an n 8 / 3 − o ⁡ ( 1 ) n^{8/3-o(1)} conditional lower bound for combinatorial algorithms on unweighted directed graphs. Chechik and Zhang [ CZ24a ] subsequently gave the first truly subcubic combinatorial algorithm for unweighted directed graphs, with running time O ~ ​ ( n 3 − 1 / 18 ) \tilde{O}(n^{3-1/18}) . For algebraic algorithms, they also obtained a O ~ ​ ( M ​ n 2.8716 ) \tilde{O}(Mn^{2.8716}) -time algorithm for edge weights in { − M , … , M } \{-M,\ldots,M\} . Thus, for combinatorial algorithms on unweighted directed graphs, there remains a substantial gap between the known upper and lower bounds. In contrast, for undirected graphs, Nogler and Vassilevska Williams [ NV26 ] recently reduced 2-FRP to single source replacement paths, yielding a O ~ ​ ( m ​ n + n 2 ) \tilde{O}(m\sqrt{n}+n^{2}) -time algorithm for unweighted graphs. They left open whether a similar reduction, possibly in a weaker form, can be obtained for directed graphs. We note that, although 2-FRP considers all pairs of failed edges, its output size is only Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Theta(n^{2}) ; see Section 2.2 for details.

sections.heading: 1.1 Our Results
sections.text: Table 1 summarizes the best known upper and lower bounds for RP and 2-FRP, together with our new results. Our first result is a simple deterministic algorithm for the RP problem. Theorem 1 . There is a deterministic combinatorial algorithm for the RP problem on unweighted directed graphs that runs in O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(m\sqrt{n}) time. The running time in Theorem 1 is optimal up to an n o ⁡ ( 1 ) n^{o(1)} factor among combinatorial algorithms [ WW18 ] , and removes the logarithmic overhead in the previous randomized and deterministic algorithms [ RZ12 , ACC19 ] . More importantly, our derandomization is considerably simpler. The randomized algorithm of Roditty and Zwick [ RZ12 ] is conceptually simple, whereas its derandomization by Alon, Chechik, and Cohen [ ACC19 ] requires substantially more machinery, including the construction of critical paths using decremental shortest-path techniques and a greedy hitting-set procedure. To obtain a simpler deterministic algorithm, we introduce a new technique, which we call a modulo-layer hitting set . The idea is extremely simple. After performing BFS from s s , we partition the vertices into L = Θ ⁡ ( n ) L=\Theta(\sqrt{n}) classes according to their distances from s s modulo L L , and use a smallest class, which has size at most n / L = O ⁡ ( n ) n/L=O(\sqrt{n}) , as the hitting set. We believe that the resulting algorithm is simple enough for textbook presentation and practical implementation. Combined with the reduction of Roditty and Zwick [ RZ12 ] , Theorem 1 also yields an efficient algorithm for computing the k k shortest simple s s – t t paths. Corollary 2 . There is a deterministic combinatorial algorithm for the k k simple shortest paths problem on unweighted directed graphs that runs in O ⁡ ( k ​ m ​ n ) O(km\sqrt{n}) time. Roditty and Zwick [ RZ12 ] reduced the k k simple shortest paths problem to O ⁡ ( k ) O(k) instances of the replacement paths problem. Thus, Corollary 2 follows from Theorem 1 without any logarithmic overhead. Our second result is a faster combinatorial algorithm for the 2-FRP problem. Our algorithm builds on our new modulo-layer hitting-set technique introduced for RP and combines it with additional ideas. Theorem 3 . There is a randomized combinatorial algorithm for the 2-FRP problem on unweighted directed graphs that runs in O ~ ​ ( n 3 − 1 / 4 ) \tilde{O}(n^{3-1/4}) time. Our algorithm improves the previous combinatorial bound O ~ ​ ( n 3 − 1 / 18 ) \tilde{O}(n^{3-1/18}) and is simpler than the previous algorithm of Chechik and Zhang [ CZ24a ] . Our algorithm also reduces directed 2-FRP to a collection of multiple-source replacement paths (MSRP) instances. This reduction can be viewed as a partial answer to the question of Nogler and Vassilevska Williams [ NV26 ] . We then solve the resulting MSRP instances using the recent algorithm of Harada and Izumi [ HI26 ] for directed graphs. Our results demonstrate that our new modulo-layer hitting-set technique is useful for both directed RP and 2-FRP. sections.heading: 1.2 Additional Related Work
sections.text: Fast algorithms for replacement paths have also been studied on special graph classes, including planar graphs [ EPR10 , WN10 ] and surface embedded graphs [ EN11 ] . Another line of work considers fast approximation algorithms [ Ber10 , CZ24b ] . The replacement paths problem has been studied in distributed settings [ MR24 , CCD+25 ] . A closely related line of work studies distance sensitivity oracles (DSOs), which can be viewed as a data-structure version of replacement paths. After preprocessing a graph, a DSO answers shortest-path distance queries efficiently under edge or vertex failures. DSOs have also been extensively studied in the literature [ BK09 , GW19 , CC20 , GR21 , Ren22 , DR22 , KS23 , DG24 , HKIM24 ] .

sections.heading: (Single-Failure) Replacement Paths (RP).
sections.text: Given a directed graph G G , two vertices s , t s,t , and a shortest s s – t t path π \pi , the replacement paths (RP) problem asks to compute 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 G ∖ e ​ ( s , t ) \mathsf{dist}_{G\setminus e}(s,t) for every edge e ∈ E e\in E . It suffices to consider edges on π \pi , since removing an edge outside π \pi does not change the s s – t t distance. Since π \pi contains at most n − 1 n-1 edges, the output size of RP is O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) .

sections.heading: Dual-Failure Replacement Paths (2-FRP).
sections.text: The dual-failure replacement paths (2-FRP) problem extends RP to two edge failures. The goal is to compute 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 G ∖ { e , e ′ } ​ ( s , t ) \mathsf{dist}_{G\setminus\{e,e^{\prime}\}}(s,t) for every pair of edges e , e ′ ∈ E e,e^{\prime}\in E . Although there are O ⁡ ( m 2 ) O(m^{2}) possible pairs of failed edges, the output size of 2-FRP is only O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) . Indeed, it suffices to consider e ∈ E ⁡ ( π ) e\in E(\pi) and, for each such edge e e , only the edges e ′ e^{\prime} on a shortest s s – t t path in G ∖ e G\setminus e . All other distances are equal to either 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 G ​ ( s , t ) \mathsf{dist}_{G}(s,t) or 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 G ∖ e ​ ( s , t ) \mathsf{dist}_{G\setminus e}(s,t) . Thus, only O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) nontrivial output values need to be represented.

sections.heading: 2.3 Multiple Source Replacement Paths
sections.text: In the multiple source replacement paths (MSRP) problem, we are given a graph and a set S S of σ \sigma sources. For every source u ∈ S u\in S , a shortest-path tree T u T_{u} rooted at u u is fixed, and the output consists of the distances 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 G ∖ e ​ ( u , v ) \mathsf{dist}_{G\setminus e}(u,v) for all v v and all edges e e on the tree path T u ​ [ u , v ] T_{u}[u,v] . For e ∉ E ⁡ ( T u ​ [ u , v ] ) e\notin E(T_{u}[u,v]) the tree path survives, so 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 G ∖ e ​ ( u , v ) = 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 G ​ ( u , v ) \mathsf{dist}_{G\setminus e}(u,v)=\mathsf{dist}_{G}(u,v) . The case σ = 1 \sigma=1 is the single source replacement paths SSRP problem. Lemma 4 (Theorem 1 of [ HI26 ] ) . MSRP on unweighted directed graphs can be solved by a randomized combinatorial algorithm in O ~ ​ ( m ​ σ ​ n + σ ​ n 2 ) \tilde{O}(m\sqrt{\sigma n}+\sigma n^{2}) time, with all output distances correct with high probability. In particular, setting σ = 1 \sigma=1 gives an O ~ ​ ( m ​ n + n 2 ) \tilde{O}(m\sqrt{n}+n^{2}) -time algorithm for SSRP.

sections.heading: 2.4 2-FRP for Weighted Directed Graphs
sections.text: Our 2-FRP algorithm reduces groups of failure pairs to small weighted instances, on which we run the algorithm of Vassilevska Williams, Woldeghebriel, and Xu [ VWX22 ] as a black box. They proposed algorithms for 2-FRP on an n n -vertex directed graph with integer edge weights and no negative cycles in O ⁡ ( n 3 ​ log 2 ​ n ) O(n^{3}\log^{2}n) time deterministically, or in O ⁡ ( n 3 ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n^{3}\log n) time with high probability. Lemma 5 (Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4 of [ VWX22 ] ) . Let G G be a directed graph with n n vertices, polynomially bounded integer edge weights, and no negative cycles, let s , t ∈ V ⁡ ( G ) s,t\in V(G) , and let π \pi be a shortest s s – t t path in G G given as part of the input. The distances 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 G ∖ { e , e ′ } ​ ( s , t ) \mathsf{dist}_{G\setminus\{e,e^{\prime}\}}(s,t) for all pairs of edges e , e ′ ∈ E ⁡ ( π ) e,e^{\prime}\in E(\pi) can be computed by a deterministic combinatorial algorithm in O ~ ​ ( n 3 ) \tilde{O}(n^{3}) time.

sections.heading: 2.5 Canonical Replacement Paths
sections.text: We use the notion of a canonical replacement path introduced in [ VWX22 ] ; see also [ CZ24a , Definition 3 in the conference version] . Definition 6 (Canonical path) . Let π \pi be a shortest s s – t t path, and let F ⊆ E F\subseteq E be a set of failed edges. An s s – t t path ρ \rho in G ∖ F G\setminus F is canonical with respect to π \pi and F F if, for any u , v ∈ V ⁡ ( π ) ∩ V ⁡ ( ρ ) u,v\in V(\pi)\cap V(\rho) such that u u appears before v v in both π , ρ \pi,\rho and E ⁡ ( π ⁡ [ u , v ] ) ∩ F = ∅ E(\pi[u,v])\cap F=\emptyset , then ρ ⁡ [ u , v ] \rho[u,v] is the same as π ⁡ [ u , v ] \pi[u,v] . Throughout the paper, in both the single-failure and dual-failure settings, whenever we consider a shortest replacement path, we choose it to be canonical. Such a canonical shortest replacement path always exists. Indeed, among all shortest s s – t t paths in G ∖ F G\setminus F , choose ρ \rho minimizing | E ⁡ ( ρ ) ∖ E ⁡ ( π ) | |E(\rho)\setminus E(\pi)| . If ρ \rho is not canonical, then for some violating pair u , v u,v , replacing ρ ⁡ [ u , v ] \rho[u,v] by π ⁡ [ u , v ] \pi[u,v] yields another shortest s s – t t path with fewer edges outside π \pi , which contradicts the choice of ρ \rho .

sections.heading: 3 Our New Simple Deterministic Algorithm for RP
sections.text: We first introduce our new derandomization technique for the RP problem, which we call a modulo-layer hitting set . The same technique will later be applied to the 2-FRP problem. By Lemma 7 , a central task in designing fast RP algorithms is to efficiently compute the detour distances 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 H ​ ( v a , v b ) \mathsf{dist}_{H}(v_{a},v_{b}) for pairs of vertices v a , v b ∈ V ⁡ ( π ) v_{a},v_{b}\in V(\pi) . Since there can be Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Theta(n^{2}) such pairs, these distances are usually not computed explicitly. Instead, they are computed implicitly. We first briefly review how previous algorithms handle these detours, and then describe our approach based on the modulo-layer hitting-set technique.

sections.heading: Previous randomized approach [ RZ12 ] .
sections.text: The randomized algorithm of Roditty and Zwick [ RZ12 ] is conceptually simple. It distinguishes replacement paths whose detour has at most ⌈ n ⌉ \lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil edges from those whose detour has more than ⌈ n ⌉ \lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil edges. Short detours are found deterministically. For long detours, a set ℛ \mathcal{R} of pivots is chosen by including every vertex independently with probability c ​ log ⁡ n / n c\log n/\sqrt{n} for a sufficiently large constant c c , and the distances in H H between the vertices of π \pi are computed by a BFS in each direction from every pivot. Since a long detour has more than ⌈ n ⌉ \lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil vertices, with high probability every long detour contains a pivot. Consequently, for every long detour from v a v_{a} to v b v_{b} , we have 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 H ​ ( v a , v b ) = min r ∈ ℛ ⁡ { 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 H ​ ( v a , r ) + 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 H ​ ( r , v b ) } . \mathsf{dist}_{H}(v_{a},v_{b})=\min_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\left\{\mathsf{dist}_{H}(v_{a},r)+\mathsf{dist}_{H}(r,v_{b})\right\}.

sections.heading: Previous deterministic approach [ ACC19 ] .
sections.text: Derandomizing the pivot-selection step above is substantially more technically challenging. Alon, Chechik, and Cohen [ ACC19 ] obtained the first deterministic O ⁡ ( m ​ n ​ log ⁡ n ) O(m\sqrt{n}\log n) -time algorithm. Their proof and algorithm require constructing a carefully chosen family of O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) critical paths, each path containing ⌈ n ⌉ \lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil edges. Computing this family efficiently requires a variant of the decremental single-source shortest-path algorithm of King [ Kin99 ] . They then apply a greedy hitting-set procedure to the family of critical paths, obtaining a set of O ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ n ) O(\sqrt{n}\log n) pivots that hits every critical path. These pivots are subsequently used within the framework of Roditty and Zwick [ RZ12 ] . The logarithmic factors in the size of the hitting set and in its computation account for the O ~ ​ ( ⋅ ) \tilde{O}(\cdot) in the running time.

sections.heading: Overview of our approach.
sections.text: Our underlying idea is entirely different, and both the algorithm and its analysis are remarkably simple. The key difference is that we do not classify detours by their length, as in [ RZ12 , ACC19 ] ; instead, we classify them by whether they pass through the hitting set or stay within a small range of consecutive BFS layers from s s , which we call a block (defined below). Instead of constructing a hitting set for a carefully chosen family of critical paths, we obtain one directly from a single BFS from s s . We group the vertices by their distance from s s modulo a parameter L = Θ ⁡ ( n ) L=\Theta(\sqrt{n}) , and let ℛ \mathcal{R} consist of the vertices in a smallest group, which has size at most n / L = O ⁡ ( n ) n/L=O(\sqrt{n}) . In other words, for some 0 ≤ ℓ ⋆ < L 0\leq\ell^{\star}<L , ℛ \mathcal{R} is the union of the BFS layers at distances h q := ℓ ⋆ + q ​ L h_{q}:=\ell^{\star}+qL from s s ( q ≥ 0 q\geq 0 ), where the BFS layer at distance d d is the set of vertices at distance exactly d d from s s ; we call these layers the separator layers . A block consists of two consecutive separator layers and all layers between them, i.e., the vertices at distances h q − 1 , h q − 1 + 1 , … , h q h_{q-1},h_{q-1}+1,\dots,h_{q} from s s for some q ≥ 0 q\geq 0 ; see Figure 2 for an illustration. Using this structural property, we show that every detour either visits a separator layer, i.e., contains a vertex of ℛ \mathcal{R} , or stays inside a single block. Thus, ℛ \mathcal{R} serves as a hitting set for all detours that leave their block. Accordingly, the detour distances can be evaluated using two kinds of BFSs: detours of the former kind are handled by BFSs from and to every vertex of ℛ \mathcal{R} in H H , which take O ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ n / L ) O((m+n)n/L) time in total, and detours of the latter kind by BFSs inside each block from the vertices of π \pi in it, which take O ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ L ) O((m+n)L) time in total. sections.heading: 4 Our Improved Combinatorial Algorithm for 2-FRP
sections.text: In this section, we present our improved combinatorial algorithm for the 2-FRP problem. We divide the cases into two based on the position of the two failed edges e , e ′ e,e^{\prime} as follows: (1) One failure on π \pi : e ∈ E ⁡ ( π ) , e ′ ∉ E ⁡ ( π ) e\in E(\pi),e^{\prime}\notin E(\pi) (2) Both failures on π \pi : e , e ′ ∈ E ⁡ ( π ) e,e^{\prime}\in E(\pi) The first case is discussed in Section 4.1 , and the second case in Section 4.2 . In both cases, we use the modulo-layer hitting set and the modulo-layer decomposition ( Section 3.1 ), which is the key to making our algorithm faster and simpler than that of Chechik and Zhang [ CZ24a ] . Note that we do not consider the case of e , e ′ ∉ E ⁡ ( π ) e,e^{\prime}\notin E(\pi) because π \pi is the shortest in this situation. Also, in the first case, we only consider e ′ e^{\prime} on the shortest s s – t t path in G ∖ e G\setminus e . More precisely, for e ∈ E ⁡ ( π ) e\in E(\pi) , let ρ e \rho_{e} be a fixed shortest s s – t t path in G ∖ e G\setminus e , that is, a replacement path for e e . Then, we consider e ′ ∈ E ⁡ ( ρ e ) ∖ E ⁡ ( π ) e^{\prime}\in E(\rho_{e})\setminus E(\pi) .

sections.heading: 5 Concluding Remarks
sections.text: In this work, we introduced the modulo-layer hitting set technique and showed that this simple idea is useful for both single-failure and dual-failure replacement paths in unweighted directed graphs. For RP, in particular, it leads to a remarkably simple deterministic algorithm that is suitable for textbook presentation and practical implementation. We believe that this technique may be useful more broadly in other shortest-path problems. For 2-FRP, the modulo-layer hitting-set technique allows us to solve the problem using MSRP and SSRP as subroutines. Our algorithm can be viewed as a weak form of a reduction from directed 2-FRP to MSRP and SSRP. Roughly speaking, our algorithm reduces directed 2-FRP to a constant number of MSRP instances with O ⁡ ( n ) O(\sqrt{n}) sources and O ⁡ ( n 1 / 4 ) O(n^{1/4}) SSRP instances. Finally, the only randomization in our 2-FRP algorithm comes from the MSRP algorithm by Harada and Izumi [ HI26 ] . Thus, a deterministic MSRP algorithm with the same running time as that of Harada and Izumi would immediately yield a deterministic O ~ ​ ( n 3 − 1 / 4 ) \tilde{O}(n^{3-1/4}) -time algorithm for 2-FRP.

Tatsuya Terao Affiliation: Kyoto University Email: ttatsuya@kurims.kyoto-u.ac.jp Abstract We study the replacement paths problem in unweighted directed graphs with n n vertices and m m edges under one or two edge failures. We give simpler and faster algorithms for both settings. Both algorithms are based on a new technique, which we call modulo-layer hitting sets . For the single-failure setting, we obtain a simple deterministic combinatorial algorithm running in O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(m\sqrt{n}) time, which is nearly optimal under the combinatorial Boolean Matrix Multiplication (BMM) conjecture. In addition to removing the logarithmic overhead of the deterministic O ~ ​ ( m ​ n ) 	ilde{O}(m\sqrt{n}) -time † † † The O ~ ​ ( ⋅ ) 	ilde{O}(\cdot) notation hides polylogarithmic factors, i.e., O ~ ​ ( f ⁡ ( n ) ) = O ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( n ) ​ polylog ​ ( n ) ) 	ilde{O}(f(n))=O(f(n)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)) . algorithm of Alon, Chechik, and Cohen [ICALP’19], our algorithm admits a much simpler implementation and analysis. For the dual-failure setting, we obtain a randomized combinatorial algorithm running in O ~ ​ ( n 3 − 1 / 4 ) 	ilde{O}(n^{3-1/4}) time. This improves upon the previous O ~ ​ ( n 3 − 1 / 18 ) 	ilde{O}(n^{3-1/18}) -time combinatorial algorithm of Chechik and Zhang [ICALP’24]. 1 Introduction In the replacement paths problem, we study how shortest paths change under edge failure. Specifically, given an unweighted directed graph G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) with n n vertices and m m edges and two vertices s , t ∈ V s,t\in V , the classical replacement paths (RP) problem asks to compute, for every edge e ∈ E e\in E , a shortest s s - t t path that avoids e e . Its natural two-failure extension, the dual-failure replacement paths (2-FRP) problem, asks to compute, for every pair of edges e , e ′ ∈ E e,e^{\prime}\in E , a shortest s s - t t path that avoids both e e and e ′ e^{\prime} . The replacement paths problem has been extensively studied in the literature [ MMG89 , NPW01 , HSB07 , GL09 , EPR10 , WN10 , Ber10 , EN11 , Wil11 , RZ12 , WY13 , LL14 , GW19 , CN20 , VWX22 , CZ24a , MR24 , CCD+25 , NV26 , HI26 ] , motivated in part by its role as a basic model for fault-tolerant routing. In real-world networks, links may become unavailable due to failures, and it is desirable to quickly find alternative routes while preserving shortest-path guarantees. Replacement paths naturally capture this task by computing shortest routes that remain available after such failures. Beyond this networking motivation, replacement paths are also closely connected to several fundamental problems. In particular, replacement paths arise in computing Vickrey pricing for shortest paths in algorithmic mechanism design (see [ NR99 , HS01 ] ). They are also closely related to the k k shortest paths problem, which is itself a classical and well-studied problem [ Law72 , Epp98 ] . For the classical RP problem, the complexity differs significantly between undirected and directed graphs. Note that the output size of RP is only Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(n) , since it suffices to consider failures of edges on a fixed shortest s s – t t path. For undirected graphs, RP can be solved essentially as efficiently as single-source shortest paths [ MMG89 , LL14 ] . In contrast, RP on directed graphs appears substantially harder. For unweighted directed graphs, Roditty and Zwick [ RZ12 ] gave a randomized combinatorial algorithm running in O ~ ​ ( m ​ n ) 	ilde{O}(m\sqrt{n}) time. Obtaining a deterministic algorithm with a comparable running time remained open for more than a decade, until Alon, Chechik, and Cohen [ ACC19 ] gave a deterministic O ~ ​ ( m ​ n ) 	ilde{O}(m\sqrt{n}) -time combinatorial algorithm. This running time is optimal up to n o ⁡ ( 1 ) n^{o(1)} factor among combinatorial algorithms, assuming the combinatorial Boolean Matrix Multiplication (BMM) conjecture [ WW18 ] . For weighted directed graphs, RP is subcubic-equivalent to APSP [ WW18 ] . ‡ ‡ ‡ Very recently, Alman and Vassilevska Williams [ AW26 ] gave a truly subcubic O ⁡ ( n 2.9995 ) O(n^{2.9995}) -time algorithm for APSP on directed graphs with polynomially bounded integer weights, refuting the APSP hypothesis. By the subcubic equivalence [ WW18 ] , RP on weighted directed graphs is thus also solvable in truly subcubic time. Their algorithm relies on fast matrix multiplication and is not combinatorial. In particular, the conditional lower bounds in this paper based on the combinatorial BMM conjecture are unaffected. For algebraic algorithms, Vassilevska Williams [ Wil11 ] gave a randomized O ~ ​ ( M ​ n ω ) 	ilde{O}(Mn^{\omega}) -time algorithm § § § Here, ω \omega denotes the exponent of square matrix multiplication. The current best bound over an arbitrary fixed field is ω < 2.37106 \omega<2.37106 [ ADV+25 , DEK+26 , Ope26a ] . Over the complex numbers, the stronger bound ω ⁡ ( ℂ ) ≤ 9 / 4 \omega(\mathbb{C})\leq 9/4 was recently established [ Ope26b ] . for edge weights in { − M , … , M } \{-M,\ldots,M\} . Although the notion of a “combinatorial algorithm” is not formally defined, here and throughout we use the term informally to refer to algorithms that do not rely on fast matrix multiplication, such as Strassen-like methods. Such algorithms are often viewed as more efficient in practice, since fast matrix multiplication algorithms typically involve large hidden constants. We refer the reader to [ AFK+24 , Section 1.1] for a more extensive discussion of the motivations for seeking combinatorial algorithms, as well as for possible operational definitions of this notion. The 2-FRP problem is considerably less understood. Vassilevska Williams, Woldeghebriel, and Xu [ VWX22 ] gave a O ~ ​ ( n 3 ) 	ilde{O}(n^{3}) -time algorithm for weighted directed graphs and an n 8 / 3 − o ⁡ ( 1 ) n^{8/3-o(1)} conditional lower bound for combinatorial algorithms on unweighted directed graphs. Chechik and Zhang [ CZ24a ] subsequently gave the first truly subcubic combinatorial algorithm for unweighted directed graphs, with running time O ~ ​ ( n 3 − 1 / 18 ) 	ilde{O}(n^{3-1/18}) . For algebraic algorithms, they also obtained a O ~ ​ ( M ​ n 2.8716 ) 	ilde{O}(Mn^{2.8716}) -time algorithm for edge weights in { − M , … , M } \{-M,\ldots,M\} . Thus, for combinatorial algorithms on unweighted directed graphs, there remains a substantial gap between the known upper and lower bounds. In contrast, for undirected graphs, Nogler and Vassilevska Williams [ NV26 ] recently reduced 2-FRP to single source replacement paths, yielding a O ~ ​ ( m ​ n + n 2 ) 	ilde{O}(m\sqrt{n}+n^{2}) -time algorithm for unweighted graphs. They left open whether a similar reduction, possibly in a weaker form, can be obtained for directed graphs. We note that, although 2-FRP considers all pairs of failed edges, its output size is only Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Theta(n^{2}) ; see Section 2.2 for details. 1.1 Our Results Table 1 summarizes the best known upper and lower bounds for RP and 2-FRP, together with our new results. Our first result is a simple deterministic algorithm for the RP problem. Theorem 1 . There is a deterministic combinatorial algorithm for the RP problem on unweighted directed graphs that runs in O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(m\sqrt{n}) time. The running time in Theorem 1 is optimal up to an n o ⁡ ( 1 ) n^{o(1)} factor among combinatorial algorithms [ WW18 ] , and removes the logarithmic overhead in the previous randomized and deterministic algorithms [ RZ12 , ACC19 ] . More importantly, our derandomization is considerably simpler. The randomized algorithm of Roditty and Zwick [ RZ12 ] is conceptually simple, whereas its derandomization by Alon, Chechik, and Cohen [ ACC19 ] requires substantially more machinery, including the construction of critical paths using decremental shortest-path techniques and a greedy hitting-set procedure. To obtain a simpler deterministic algorithm, we introduce a new technique, which we call a modulo-layer hitting set . The idea is extremely simple. After performing BFS from s s , we partition the vertices into L = Θ ⁡ ( n ) L=\Theta(\sqrt{n}) classes according to their distances from s s modulo L L , and use a smallest class, which has size at most n / L = O ⁡ ( n ) n/L=O(\sqrt{n}) , as the hitting set. We believe that the resulting algorithm is simple enough for textbook presentation and practical implementation. Combined with the reduction of Roditty and Zwick [ RZ12 ] , Theorem 1 also yields an efficient algorithm for computing the k k shortest simple s s – t t paths. Corollary 2 . There is a deterministic combinatorial algorithm for the k k simple shortest paths problem on unweighted directed graphs that runs in O ⁡ ( k ​ m ​ n ) O(km\sqrt{n}) time. Roditty and Zwick [ RZ12 ] reduced the k k simple shortest paths problem to O ⁡ ( k ) O(k) instances of the replacement paths problem. Thus, Corollary 2 follows from Theorem 1 without any logarithmic overhead. Our second result is a faster combinatorial algorithm for the 2-FRP problem. Our algorithm builds on our new modulo-layer hitting-set technique introduced for RP and combines it with additional ideas. Theorem 3 . There is a randomized combinatorial algorithm for the 2-FRP problem on unweighted directed graphs that runs in O ~ ​ ( n 3 − 1 / 4 ) 	ilde{O}(n^{3-1/4}) time. Our algorithm improves the previous combinatorial bound O ~ ​ ( n 3 − 1 / 18 ) 	ilde{O}(n^{3-1/18}) and is simpler than the previous algorithm of Chechik and Zhang [ CZ24a ] . Our algorithm also reduces directed 2-FRP to a collection of multiple-source replacement paths (MSRP) instances. This reduction can be viewed as a partial answer to the question of Nogler and Vassilevska Williams [ NV26 ] . We then solve the resulting MSRP instances using the recent algorithm of Harada and Izumi [ HI26 ] for directed graphs. Our results demonstrate that our new modulo-layer hitting-set technique is useful for both directed RP and 2-FRP.
